title: Strings on the heap
lesson:
A C string is an array of `char` that ends with a zero byte, `'\0'`. That zero is how every string function knows where the text stops. `"maize"` takes **6** bytes: five letters and the `'\0'`.

`strlen` counts the letters but **not** the `'\0'`. So when you put a copy of a string on the heap, you need `strlen(s) + 1` bytes. Forgetting the `+ 1` is the classic C string bug: the copy works most of the time, then one day the missing zero lets `printf` run off into whatever is next in memory.

```
char *str_copy(const char *s)
{
    size_t n = strlen(s);
    char *copy = malloc(n + 1);       /* + 1 for the '\0' */
    if (copy == NULL) return NULL;
    memcpy(copy, s, n + 1);           /* copies the '\0' too */
    return copy;                      /* caller frees it */
}
```

Why copy at all? A name typed by the user often sits in a buffer that gets reused for the next line. If you only keep a pointer to that buffer, your saved name changes under you. A heap copy belongs to you.

**strdup isn't standard C.** Linux has `strdup`, Windows calls it `_strdup`, and C11 doesn't promise either. Writing your own `str_copy` is five lines and works everywhere, so that's what we do.

**Joining strings** works the same way: add up the lengths, allocate once with `+ 1`, then copy each piece in at the right place. `memcpy(dest + offset, piece, len)` is cleaner than chains of `strcat`, which re-scan the string every time.

**Splitting a line** like `Amina,maize,40` into fields:
1. Count the separators: fields = separators + 1.
2. Allocate an array of `char *`, one per field.
3. For each field, find where it ends (the next separator or `'\0'`), allocate `length + 1`, copy the letters, add the `'\0'`.

The result is a block holding pointers to other blocks, so freeing takes two steps: free every field, *then* the array. Do it the other way round and you can no longer reach the fields.

**Who frees?** Every function that returns new memory should say so in its comment: "the caller frees it". That one line of documentation prevents most leaks in real C projects.

**Don't return a local buffer.** `char buf[64]; ... return buf;` hands back memory that disappears when the function ends. Return heap memory, or have the caller pass in a buffer and its size.

CSV logs, config files, commands arriving over a serial line from a robot: they all start with copying and splitting strings like this.

notes: str_copy allocates strlen(s) + 1 bytes: the + 1 is for the '\0'.
memcpy with n + 1 copies the letters and the terminating zero in one go.
The comment says who frees the result: the caller.
Reusing line doesn't change saved, because saved is its own copy.
main frees saved once it's done with it.

exercises.title: Your own strdup
exercises.prompt: Write char *str_copy(const char *s): a new heap copy of s, allocated with my_alloc using exactly strlen(s) + 1 bytes, including the '\0'. The caller frees it. If s is NULL, return NULL.

tests.call: ({ char *c = str_copy("Amina"); static char b[64]; strcpy(b, c); my_free(c); b; })
tests.name: copies the text

tests.call: ({ char *c = str_copy("maize"); int r = (int)last_alloc_size; my_free(c); r; })
tests.name: exactly strlen + 1 bytes
tests.hint_if_fail: 5 letters need 6 bytes: one more for the '\0'.

tests.call: ({ char src[] = "beans"; char *c = str_copy(src); src[0] = 'X'; static char b[64]; strcpy(b, c); my_free(c); b; })
tests.name: a separate copy

tests.call: ({ char *c = str_copy(""); int r = (int)last_alloc_size * 10 + (c[0] == 0); my_free(c); r; })
tests.name: empty string still needs 1 byte

hints: Check for NULL (both s and the result).
memcpy(copy, s, n + 1); copies the '\0' too.

exercises.title: Join with a separator
exercises.prompt: Write char *join(const char *a, const char *sep, const char *b): a new heap string a + sep + b, made with ONE my_alloc of exactly the right size (all three lengths + 1). The caller frees it. join("Juma", ", ", "Otieno") gives "Juma, Otieno".

tests.call: ({ char *j = join("Juma", ", ", "Otieno"); static char b[64]; strcpy(b, j); my_free(j); b; })
tests.name: joins three parts

tests.call: ({ char *j = join("Juma", ", ", "Otieno"); int r = (int)last_alloc_size; my_free(j); r; })
tests.name: exactly the right size

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; char *j = join("tank", "_", "7"); int r = live_allocs - before; my_free(j); r; })
tests.name: one allocation

tests.call: ({ char *j = join("", "-", ""); static char b[8]; strcpy(b, j); my_free(j); b; })
tests.name: empty parts

tests.call: ({ char *j = join("maize", "", ""); static char b[16]; strcpy(b, j); my_free(j); b; })
tests.name: empty separator

hints: Get la, ls, lb with strlen, then my_alloc(la + ls + lb + 1).
memcpy(out, a, la); memcpy(out + la, sep, ls); memcpy(out + la + ls, b, lb);

exercises.title: Split a CSV line
exercises.prompt: Write char **split(const char *line, char sep, int *count). Return a new heap array of new heap strings, one per field, and store the number of fields in *count. There is always one more field than there are separators, so "a,,b" gives 3 fields (the middle one is "") and "" gives 1 empty field. Use my_alloc for everything; free_fields (given) frees the result. If memory runs out, free what you made, set *count to 0 and return NULL.

tests.call: ({ int n; char **f = split("Amina,maize,40", ',', &n); free_fields(f, n); n; })
tests.name: counts the fields

tests.call: ({ int n; char **f = split("Amina,maize,40", ',', &n); static char b[64]; strcpy(b, f[1]); free_fields(f, n); b; })
tests.name: middle field

tests.call: ({ int n; char **f = split("Amina,maize,40", ',', &n); static char b[64]; strcpy(b, f[2]); free_fields(f, n); b; })
tests.name: last field
tests.hint_if_fail: The last field ends at the '\0', not at a separator.

tests.call: ({ int n; char **f = split("a,,b", ',', &n); int r = n * 10 + (f[1][0] == 0); free_fields(f, n); r; })
tests.name: empty field in the middle

tests.call: ({ int n; char **f = split("Wanjiru", ';', &n); int r = n * 10 + (strcmp(f[0], "Wanjiru") == 0); free_fields(f, n); r; })
tests.name: no separator: one field

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; int n; char **f = split("x;y", ';', &n); int during = live_allocs - before; free_fields(f, n); during * 10 + (live_allocs - before); })
tests.name: one block per field plus the array, all freed

hints: First loop: count separators; fields = that + 1. Allocate n * sizeof(char *).
For each field: find its end (the next sep or '\0'), length = end - start, my_alloc(length + 1), memcpy, add '\0'.
Next field starts at end + 1. If an allocation fails, free_fields(fields, i) and return NULL.

quiz.q: How many bytes does a heap copy of "tank" need?
Why copy a name instead of keeping a pointer to the input buffer?
choices: The buffer gets reused for the next line, so the saved name would change
quiz.why: A heap copy belongs to you.

quiz.q: You split a line into a char ** of heap strings. How do you free it?
choices: Free each field, then free the array
Free the array, then each field
quiz.why: Free the array last, or you lose the way to reach the fields.

quiz.q: Why write your own str_copy instead of strdup?
choices: strdup isn't part of standard C11, so it's missing or named differently on some compilers
quiz.why: Five lines of portable code beats a missing function.

quiz.q: A function does char buf[64]; ... return buf;. What's the problem?
choices: buf disappears when the function returns
quiz.why: Return heap memory, or let the caller pass a buffer.

explain: Explain in your own words why a string copy needs strlen + 1 bytes, using a word you choose and counting its bytes.
